blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
1. Introduction
This paper is devoted to traces and characters in homotopical algebra and their application to
algebraic geometry and representation theory. We observe that many geometric ﬁxed point and
trace formulas can be expressed as linearizations of fundamental nonlinear identities, describing
dimensions and traces directly in the setting of correspondence categories of varieties or stacks.
This gives a simple uniform perspective on (and useful generalizations of) geometric character
and ﬁxed point formulas of Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch and Atiyah-Bott-Lefschetz type. In
addition, one can

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content: []{#summary label="summary"} We now describe the main theorem, extending classical trace and dimension formulas to a very general setting in derived algebraic geometry (including equivariance for arbitrary Lie algebroids or affine algebraic groups) without any smoothness or transversality assumptions, while emphasizing that the main contribution of the paper is the simple geometric formalism underlying these formulas. blocks.title: Inspirations and motivations
blocks.content: This work has many inspirations. It is heavily reliant on the $\infty$-categorical foundations of higher algebra, derived algebraic geometry and sheaf theory due to Lurie [@HA; @SAG] and Gaitsgory-Rozenblyum [@GR]. It is also inspired by Lurie's cobordism hypothesis with singularities [@TFT], which provides a powerful unifying tool for higher algebra. blocks.title: Traces in category theory
blocks.content:
We highlight structures arising in the general theory of dualizable objects in symmetric monoidal higher categories (see also [@doldpuppe; @may; @PS]). For legibility, we suppress all $\oo$-categorical notations and complications from the introduction. We rely on [@GR] for the theory of symmetric monoidal $(\oo,2)$-categories, though only the formal outline of the theory is in fact needed for this paper. See [@TV; @HSS] for thorough treatments of the theory of traces in higher category theory.

blocks.content:
To apply the preceding formalism to geometry, it is useful to organize spaces and maps within a suitable categorical framework. We then arrive at loop spaces and fixed point loci as nonlinear expressions of dimensions and traces. This simple observation provides the core of the paper. Throughout the discussion, we continue to suppress all $\oo$-categorical notations and complications. blocks.content:
[]{#sheaf intro label="sheaf intro"}

Given any sufficiently functorial method of measuring derived stacks, the preceding calculations of geometric dimensions, traces and their functoriality immediately lead to trace and character formulas. To formalize the functoriality needed, we will use the language of sheaf theories. blocks.title: Preliminaries
blocks.content:
Our working setting is the higher category theory and algebra developed by J. Lurie [@topos; @HA; @SAG], see Chapter I.1 of [@GR] for an excellent overview.

By forgetting non-invertible 2-morphisms we obtain a symmetric monoidal $(\oo,1)$-category $f(\cA)$, which we will abusively refer to as $\cA$ whenever only invertible higher morphisms are involved. For concreteness, we fix a base commutative ring, and work in the symmetric monoidal $(\oo,1)$-category $Stacks_k$ of derived stacks over $\Spec k$. Traces for sheaves
Dimensions and traces of sheaf categories: 1-categorical consequences
blocks.content:
The graph of a map of derived stacks $f:X\to Y$ provides a correspondence from $X$ to $Y$ and a correspondence from $Y$ to $X$. We denote the respective induced maps by $f_{*}:\cS(X)\to \cS(Y)$ and $f^!:\cS(Y)\to \cS(X)$. The functoriality of $\cS$ concisely encodes base change for $f_{*}$ and $f^!$. For $\pi:X\to pt = \Spec k$, we denote by $\omega_{X}=\pi^! k\in \cS(X)$ the $\cS$-analogue of the dualizing sheaf, and by $\omega(X)=\pi_{*}\omega_{X} \in \cS(pt) = dgVect_k$ the $\cS$-analogue of "global volume forms\".
